title: Cologne Cathedral took 632 years to build; a medieval crane sat on it for 400 years

cover.alt: The west façade of Cologne Cathedral: two soaring, intricately carved Gothic towers of dark stone rising above the great portal, seen from the square below.

body: The foundation stone of Cologne Cathedral was laid on 15 August 1248. Work on the south tower stopped in 1473, and on the nave during the 16th century, leaving a huge wooden crane on the half-built tower that stayed there as a landmark of the city’s skyline for 400 years. Spurred by the rediscovery of the original plan for the façade, building resumed in 1842 to the medieval drawings, with modern touches such as iron roof girders, and completion was celebrated on 15 October 1880, **632 years** after the start. Its 157 m towers made it the tallest building in the world for four years, until the Washington Monument overtook it.

slides.alt: Aerial photograph from March 1945: the twin spires of Cologne Cathedral stand amid a city of roofless, bombed-out buildings beside the Rhine.
slides.caption: March 1945: the cathedral stands amid a flattened Cologne. It was hit by fourteen aerial bombs during the war and stayed standing.

slides.question: In which year was the cathedral finally completed?
slides.explanation: 1880. Work resumed in 1842 after a pause of about three centuries on the nave and four on the south tower, following the medieval plans that had survived.

slides.label: the height of the towers, the tallest building in the world from 1880 to 1884
slides.text: The Washington Monument took the title in 1884. Germany’s most visited landmark now draws about 6 million people a year.

events.text: Work on the south tower stops

slides.question: What is kept in the cathedral’s great golden shrine?
options: A piece of the True Cross
slides.explanation: The Shrine of the Three Kings, begun in 1190 by Nicholas of Verdun, is believed to hold the remains of the Magi. It was saved from the fire of 1248 that preceded the new building.

left.text: Built by hand to the Gothic plan. The south tower reached only belfry level before work stopped, with the crane left on top.

right.text: Finished to the surviving medieval drawings, but with iron roof girders and 19th-century techniques; the towers rose to 157 m.
